title: Macros, attributes and comments
intro: A name followed by `!`, such as `println!` or `vec!`, is a macro call: the compiler expands it into other code first. An ordinary Rust function has a fixed list of parameters, so this is how `println!` takes any number of arguments and checks its format string before the program runs. A line that starts with `#[...]` is an attribute, a note to the compiler about the item below it. Comments start with `//`, and `///` turns a comment into documentation. `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` format and check the code.

coming_from.go: `fmt.Printf("%d %s", n, s)` is `println!("{} {}", n, s)`: `{}` replaces the verbs, and the compiler checks the string against the arguments. Struct tags like `json:"name"` become attributes such as `#[serde(rename = "name")]` (from the serde crate). The nearest thing to `//go:build linux` is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`, which applies to one item, not a whole file. `cargo fmt` is `gofmt`.
coming_from.kotlin: `println("$name is $age")` is `println!("{name} is {age}")`, and `"%5d".format(n)` becomes `{:5}` inside the same macro. `@Test` is `#[test]`, `@Suppress("unused")` is `#[allow(unused)]`, and what a `data class` writes for you (`toString`, `equals`) comes from `#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]`.
coming_from.python: `print(f"{name} is {age}")` is `println!("{name} is {age}")`, and the specs after the colon are close to yours (`{x:>5}`, `{x:05}`). One difference: Rust's `{x:.2}` means two decimals, where Python's `.2` alone means two significant digits. `@dataclass` is closest to `#[derive(...)]`; a decorator that wraps a function has no direct equivalent, because attributes act while the program is compiled, not when it runs.
coming_from.typescript: A template literal `${name}` is `{name}` inside `println!` or `format!`, but only a plain name goes inside the braces, not `a + b`. `/** JSDoc */` becomes `///`, and Prettier and ESLint are closest to `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy`.
coming_from.java: `System.out.printf("%5d%n", n)` is `println!("{:5}", n)`, and `println!` adds the newline for you. Annotations become attributes: `@Test` is `#[test]`, `@Deprecated` is `#[deprecated]`, `@SuppressWarnings` is `#[allow(...)]`. There is no `@Override`, and `assert!` is always on, unlike Java's `assert`.
coming_from.csharp: Attributes are in the family you know: the Rust Reference says its `#[...]` syntax comes from C#. `[Fact]` is `#[test]`, `[Obsolete]` is `#[deprecated]`, `#if DEBUG` is `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]`, and `$"{n,5}"` is `{n:5}` inside `println!`.
coming_from.c: `printf("%5.2f %d\n", x, n)` is `println!("{:5.2} {}", x, n)`: there is no `%d` or `%s`, and the compiler checks the string against the arguments, so a mismatch is always an error. (GCC warns about `printf` mismatches under `-Wall`, but the C standard still calls them undefined behaviour.) `#define` macros substitute tokens; Rust's `name!` macros receive parsed syntax.
coming_from.cpp: C++20's `std::format("{:>5}", n)` already uses `{}` placeholders like `println!` (though `{:d}` is legal there and an error in Rust). `#define` macros substitute tokens; Rust's `name!` macros receive parsed syntax. `[[nodiscard]]` and `[[deprecated]]` are `#[must_use]` and `#[deprecated]`.

notes: `name!(...)` is a macro call, not a function call. The compiler expands it before it checks types, which is how `println!` accepts any number of arguments although Rust functions cannot.
In a format string, `{}` prints with `Display`, `{:?}` with `Debug`, and a spec after the colon sets width, alignment and precision. `{{` and `}}` print one brace each.
`#[...]` applies to the item after it, and `#![...]` to the file or module it sits in. The common ones are `derive`, `test`, `allow` and `cfg`.
`//` and `/* */` are comments (block comments nest). `///` documents the item below it and `//!` the file around it; `cargo doc` builds web pages from them.
`cargo fmt` rewrites your code in the standard style, and `cargo clippy` adds more checks than the compiler runs.

gotcha.title: Using %d in a format string
gotcha.looks_fine: In C, Go, Java, Kotlin and Python, `%d` marks where a number goes. It is the format string you already know.
gotcha.rust_sees: `println!` uses braces for placeholders. It sees `%d` as plain text, finds an argument with no placeholder, and stops with `argument never used`. It even points at the fix: `{}`.
gotcha.why: Rust's format strings use `{}`, and the compiler checks that every argument has a placeholder and every placeholder has an argument. It does not know that `%d` means anything: `%d` is plain text to it, so an argument aimed at a `%d` is left without a placeholder and is rejected. (A `%d` with no argument at all compiles and prints `%d`.) The fix is `{}` with no letter: the argument's type decides how it prints, and `{:?}` asks for the debugging form. Most other languages run this program; the C# outputs show a version that runs but prints the wrong thing.

go.says: Go prints `count: 5`. `Printf` takes verbs such as `%d`.

kotlin.says: Kotlin prints `count: 5`. `"count: %d".format(count)` uses Java's format syntax.

python.says: Python prints `count: 5`. The `%` operator on a string is Python's older formatting style.

typescript.says: TypeScript prints `count: 5`. Node's `console.log` treats `%d` in the first argument as a placeholder.

java.says: Java prints `count: 5`. `printf` takes `%d`, and `%n` is the newline.

csharp.says: C# compiles this and prints `count: %d`. Its composite format strings use `{0}`, so `%d` is plain text and the extra argument is ignored, with no compiler message by default.

c.says: C prints `count: 5`. `printf` is where `%d` comes from.

cpp.says: C++ prints `count: 5` with `printf`. `std::format` (C++20) uses `{}` as Rust does, though it accepts `{:d}`, which Rust does not.

kotlin.code:
/** A point on a grid. */
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val p = Point(3, 4) // a line comment
    val items = listOf(1, 2, 3)
    check(items.size == 3) // stops with an exception if false
    println("point: Point { x: ${p.x}, y: ${p.y} }")
    println("items: $items")
    println("row: [${"%5d".format(42)}] [${"%-5d".format(42)}] [${"%05d".format(42)}]")
    val pi = "%.2f".format(3.14159)
    println("pi: $pi {done}")
}

python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    """A point on a grid."""

    x: int
    y: int


p = Point(3, 4)  # a line comment
items = [1, 2, 3]
assert len(items) == 3  # stops with an error if false
print(f"point: Point {{ x: {p.x}, y: {p.y} }}")
print(f"items: {items}")
print(f"row: [{42:>5}] [{42:<5}] [{42:05}]")
pi = f"{3.14159:.2f}"
print(f"pi: {pi} {{done}}")

check-go.go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

var bad = false

func same(got, want string) {
	if got != want {
		fmt.Printf("got [%s], want [%s]\n", got, want)
		bad = true
	}
}

func main() {
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%5d", 42), "   42")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%-5d", 42), "42   ")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%05d", 42), "00042")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%+d", 42), "+42")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%.2f", 3.14159), "3.14")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%8.3f", 3.14159), "   3.142")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%x", 255), "ff")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%#x", 255), "0xff")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%10s", "Ada"), "       Ada")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%-10s", "Ada"), "Ada       ")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%.3s", "Lovelace"), "Lov")
	same(fmt.Sprintf("%d %s", 42, "Ada"), "42 Ada")
	if bad {
		panic("a Go format row is wrong")
	}
	fmt.Println("ok")
}
